detail.abstract: What does it mean to be a good democratic citizen? We address this question by measuring citizens’ beliefs about injunctive civic norms — defined as shared expectations about how people ought to behave — in 17 democracies. We show that most people believe that good citizenship involves not only obeying rules and laws, but also contributing to the community through volunteering and civic engagement. This challenges purely utilitarian models of citizenship and theories that view citizens as "spectators"' rather than "participants". By contrast, behaviors related to support of tolerance, diversity, and pluralism are less likely to be perceived as norms that must be followed. Yet experimental data reveal strong personal preferences for such "acceptance" norms. This divergence between privately held beliefs about how citizens should behave and beliefs about others’ normative preferences is a likely source of social conflict that could weaken trust and cooperation.

title: Stop Believing in Haircuts
affiliations: University of Cologne - Department of Finance, European Central Bank (ECB) - Directorate General Market Operations and

detail.title: Stop Believing in Haircuts

keywords: MONETARY POLICY TRANSMISSION JEL CLASSIFICATION: E43

detail.abstract: We investigate how frictions in euro area repo markets distort the setting of haircuts - often presented as the main risk management tool in repo transactions. Using unique European repo data, we show that balance sheet constraints, collateral heterogeneity, and dealer market power lead to suboptimal haircuts, especially in collateral-driven repos. We develop a theoretical model explaining these distortions and their effects on market outcomes. Our findings highlight the underlying frictions behind suboptimal haircuts which result in more volatile repo rates and volumes, and have important implications for monetary policy and financial stability.

title: The Rhetorical Arms Race: Strategic Hostility and Institutional Amplification
affiliations: University of Manchester

detail.title: The Rhetorical Arms Race: Strategic Hostility and Institutional Amplification
detail.abstract: We develop a game-theoretic framework to analyze the strategic use of non-informational, hostile rhetoric in electoral competition. In a baseline setting of proportional representation, candidates engage in a "rhetorical arms race," escalating identity-based hostility to avoid ceding affective advantage despite mutual welfare losses. We generalize this model by embedding the contest within a general institutional framework that maps vote shares to political power under varying degrees of disproportionality. Under mild regularity conditions and a cost-dominance restriction, we establish the existence of a unique interior Nash equilibrium. The analysis reveals that equilibrium hostility rises with voters' affective responsiveness and falls with the cost of aggression. Crucially, we find that greater institutional disproportionality-such as winner-take-all rules-strictly amplifies hostility and magnifies the electoral impact of small asymmetries between candidates. Furthermore, the local curvature of the institutional mapping endogenously determines whether rhetorical campaign efforts function as strategic substitutes or complements. These findings characterize toxic political discourse as a predictable equilibrium outcome driven by institutional design rather than idiosyncratic behavior.

title: Political Polarization and Partisan Consumption Cycles
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: Political Polarization and Partisan Consumption Cycles
detail.abstract: Partisanship and political polarization have a substantial impact on discretionary consumption: counties aligned with the party of the sitting president increase consumption significantly more than unaligned counties. The effect size of political alignment is comparable to that of per capita income and population growth and has grown over time as Democrats and Republicans have become increasingly polarized. We show that the consumption difference between politically aligned and unaligned counties persists throughout the presidential term, consistent with a channel through which expectations influence consumer behavior and propagate through local economic activity. These findings highlight how political affiliation and polarization influence economic behavior at the local level, with broader implications for macroeconomic dynamics and both theoretical and empirical finance.

title: The Combined Effect of Door-to-Door and Pay-as-You-Throw: Evidence from Emilia-Romagna
affiliations: Joint Research Center of the European Commission, Joint Research Center of the European Commission and Joint Research Center of the European Commission

detail.title: The Combined Effect of Door-to-Door and Pay-as-You-Throw: Evidence from Emilia-Romagna
detail.abstract: This paper estimates the impact of door-to-door collection and of pay-as-you-throw tariffs on total waste and on the fraction of sorted waste generated in Emilia-Romagna, Italy, between 2016 and 2023. The analysis employs novel difference-indifferences techniques to assess the impacts of the two treatments, avoiding possible contamination caused by their interaction. Results are based on administrative monthly data from 279 municipalities, and show that DtD collection significantly increased the share of sorted waste and reduced total waste per capita. Pay-as-you-throw tariffs further enhanced sorting performance, with evidence of announcement effects preceding formal implementation, and evidence of preventing waste generation. Finally, a complementary analysis of waste quality data suggests that both policies improved sorting accuracy, particularly for paper and residual waste.

title: Fiscal Geometry and Structural Visibility in Social Analysis

detail.title: Fiscal Geometry and Structural Visibility in Social Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is conceptual and methodological in nature and does not involve human participants, personal data, or intervention. Ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: The author declares no competing interests. The views expressed are solely those of the author.

detail.abstract:
High-level social theory has developed powerful interpretive tools to analyze institutions through narrative, critique, and contextual explanation. These approaches are essential for understanding meaning, power, and lived experience, yet they often rely on dense interpretive interfaces that are difficult to audit, replicate, or compare across cases without re-entering extensive narrative terrain. This paper introduces Fiscal Geometry (FG) as a pre-interpretive methodological supplement designed to address this limitation.

FG does not seek to replace narrative analysis, critical theory, or interpretive judgment, nor does it adjudicate normative disputes. Instead, it provides a structural instrument that renders institutional interactions visible prior to interpretation by mapping how fiscal rules, classification mechanisms, and institutional interfaces organize constraint, movement, and differentiation. By emphasizing structural visibility, symmetric comparability, and reconcilability without adjudication, FG offers a neutral analytical layer that enables earlier alignment in institutional analysis without requiring premature narrative consensus.

The paper situates FG within longstanding methodological debates on interpretation, measurement, and comparison, arguing that many persistent disagreements in social analysis stem less from irreconcilable values than from the absence of a shared structural reference frame. FG is proposed as a complementary coordination layer that supports interdisciplinary dialogue, time-sensitive institutional evaluation, and cross-domain comparison while preserving the interpretive strengths of high-level social theory.

title: Sales-Based CEO Incentives and their Effect across the Supply Chain
affiliations: University of Michigan at Ann Arbor - Accounting

detail.title: Sales-Based CEO Incentives and their Effect across the Supply Chain
detail.abstract: I examine how the use of sales performance measures in CEO incentive contracts affects the operation of a firm and its suppliers. A growing number of firms are evaluating and compensating their CEOs based on sales performance. However, since sales is a narrow metric of performance that does not incentivize expenditure control, these measures can motivate operational decisions that affect not only the firm but also its suppliers. I show that sales performance measures in CEO bonus contracts generate inventory fluctuations that increase the bullwhip effect, a phenomenon whereby a firm exhibits exaggerated variability in its orders to suppliers, amplifying demand variability upstream. Instrumental variable tests using the firm’s network connections through compensation consultants suggest that the results are not driven by omitted factors. Collectively, my findings illuminate the plausible spillover effect of CEO incentive contracts on economically linked operations.

title: The Macroeconomic Effects of Tariffs: Evidence From U.S. Historical Data
affiliations: Northwestern University and Northwestern University

detail.title: The Macroeconomic Effects of Tariffs: Evidence From U.S. Historical Data
detail.abstract: We study the macroeconomic effects of tariff policy using U.S. historical data from 1840–2024. We construct a narrative series of plausibly exogenous tariff changes – based on major legislative actions, multilateral negotiations, and temporary surcharges – and use it as an instrument to identify a structural tariff shock. Tariff increases are consistently contractionary: imports fall sharply, exports decline with a lag, and output and manufacturing activity drop persistently. The shock transmits through both supply and demand channels. Prices rise in the full sample but fall post-WWII, a pattern consistent with changes in the monetary policy response and with stronger international retaliation and reciprocity in the modern trade regime.

title: The Effect of Centralized-Admission School Lotteries on Between-School Segregation: Evidence from 300 Largest School Districts in the United States
affiliations: , Old Dominion University and

detail.title: The Effect of Centralized-Admission School Lotteries on Between-School Segregation: Evidence from 300 Largest School Districts in the United States

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: This study examines how centralized-admission school lotteries affect between-school racial and ethnic segregation in the largest U.S. public school districts. Using original nationwide panel data and a difference-in-differences design with staggered adoption, the research analyzes effects on school composition, intergroup exposure, and distribution evenness. The findings reveal that centralized-admission lotteries led to increased White student enrollment in district schools and modest improvements in intergroup exposure. Black-White exposure rose by 1.6 percentage points and student of color-White exposure by 1.8 points. However, White students experienced reduced exposure to all racial and ethnic groups, with similar patterns for Black, Asian, and other students of color. While centralized lotteries modestly redistribute students, they do not significantly reduce overall segregation, challenging assumptions about equity-promoting reforms. These results underscore the need for complementary policies including weighted lottery designs, transportation subsidies, and targeted adoption to address the structural roots of school segregation.

title: Online Tutoring, School Performance, and School-to-Work Transitions: Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial
affiliations: German Institute for Economic Research (DIW Berlin), Government of the Federal Republic of Germany - Institute for Employment Research (IAB), Government of the Federal Republic of Germany - Institute for Employment Research (IAB), University of Potsdam, University of Potsdam, Nuremberg Institute of Technology and University of Potsdam

detail.title: Online Tutoring, School Performance, and School-to-Work Transitions: Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Tutoring programs for low-performing students, delivered in-person or online, effectively enhance school performance, yet their medium- and longer-term impacts on labor market outcomes remain less understood. To address this gap, we conduct a randomized controlled trial with 839 secondary school students in Germany to examine the effects of an online tutoring program for low-performing students on academic performance and school-to-work transitions. The online tutoring program had a non-significant intention-to-treat effect of 0.06 standard deviations on math grades six months after program start. However, among students who had not received other tutoring services prior to the intervention, the program significantly improved math grades by 0.14 standard deviations. Moreover, students in non-academic school tracks experienced smoother school-to-work transitions, with vocational training take-up 18 months later being 5 percentage points higheran effect that was even larger (12 percentage points) among those without prior tutoring. Overall, the results indicate that tutoring can generate lasting benefits for low-performing students that extend beyond school performance.

title: From Root Causes to Shared Gains: Migration Policy for Low-Income Countries in a Labor-Scarce World
affiliations: George Mason University

detail.title: From Root Causes to Shared Gains: Migration Policy for Low-Income Countries in a Labor-Scarce World

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: International migration policy for lower-income countries is still guided by assumptions from an earlier erawhen less-educated labor was abundant, skilled emigration was seen purely as brain drain, and development was expected to reduce migration. That world is gone. This paper reviews recent research on migration policy in the 21st century, when demographic decline is making labor scarce globally, skilled emigration can yield net long- term gains for origin countries, and development often increases migration pressures for generations. The literature shows that migration, managed through innovative institutions, can sustain fiscal systems in aging economies, spur human capital investment at origin, and accelerate structural change. Migration is not a substitute for development, but a catalyst and major opportunity. Policy priorities include regional free-movement regimes, new destination-country partnerships, restructured skill-training systems for a mobile world, and integrating migration into aid partnerships. Much more research is needed to understand the impacts of these tools.

title: Estimating the Effect of Free Shipping on a Competitive Online Platform
affiliations: , Columbia University and Istanbul Technical University

detail.title: Estimating the Effect of Free Shipping on a Competitive Online Platform

declarations.funderStatement: First author's research is partially funded by TÜBİTAK (Scientific and Technological Research Council of Turkey).

detail.abstract: Sales through online platforms where many sellers compete are affected by pricing and free shipping activities. This study examines the impact of free shipping on online sales within competitive marketplaces. We acknowledge the potential endogeneity between pricing, free shipping offers, and sales volume. To address this, we employ instrumental variables in a two-stage least squares regression with panel data, controlling for fixed effects at the seller and product subcategory level. This approach mitigates bias and inconsistency arising from endogeneity. Using transaction data from a multi-seller online marketplace, we demonstrate that ignoring endogeneity leads to significantly biased estimates. Our carefully designed identification strategy for the data at hand, suggests that a 10% increase in daily free shipping offers can increase sales (by approximately 15%) and revenue (by approximately 24%). However, free shipping also incurs costs. We argue that platform owners operating as resellers have an advantage in optimizing free shipping strategies across multiple categories compared to third-party sellers who may not have a presence in all categories. This study highlights the importance of considering endogeneity between price, free shipping, and sales in competitive online platforms. Our results suggest that free shipping can be a powerful tool for boosting sales and revenue, but its effectiveness depends on profit margins. When margins are tight, the cost of free shipping may outweigh the benefits.

title: Copyright and Condemnation
affiliations: University of Technology Sydney, Faculty of Law

detail.title: Copyright and Condemnation

publicationDetails.detailsText: Australian Intellectual Property Journal, Volume 36, Issue 2, 117-132

detail.abstract: In a recent decision, the Full Court of the Federal Court of Australia declared a constructive trust over a trespassing filmmaker's copyright to effect specific restitution of that copyright to the landowner victim of the trespass. This provided a basis to grant permanent injunctive relief to suppress the film. Given that the filmmaker was an animal liberationist organisation, and the landowner was an abattoir, the trust raises complex issues of civics. After considering the character and consequences of the declared trust, this piece argues that the issues of civics the trust implicates can only be properly addressed if its imposition is governed by judicial discretion.

title: The Long Shadow of Labor Market Entry Conditions: Intergenerational Determinants of Mental Health
affiliations: Banco de España, CEMFI and

detail.title: The Long Shadow of Labor Market Entry Conditions: Intergenerational Determinants of Mental Health

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: What determines long-term mental health and its intergenerational correlation? Exploiting variation in unemployment rates upon labor market entry across Australian states and cohorts, we provide novel evidence that the mental health of daughters is affected by the labor market entry conditions of their parents. In particular, a one standard deviation shock to the unemployment rate upon parental labor market entry worsens daughters' mental health during adolescence by 11% of a standard deviation. This effect is accompanied by lower levels of satisfaction with their health, financial situation, safety, and overall life. A mediation analysis suggests that a sizable proportion (24%) of the impacts on the descendants' mental health is explained by the worse mental health of their parents at mid-life. We do not detect any systematic impact of parental labor market entry conditions among sons.

title: How to Attract Talent? Field-Experimental Evidence on Emphasizing Flexibility and Career Opportunities in Job Advertisements
affiliations: University of Cologne, University of Cologne - Department of Personnel Economics, University of Cologne and University of Cologne

detail.title: How to Attract Talent? Field-Experimental Evidence on Emphasizing Flexibility and Career Opportunities in Job Advertisements

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: We conduct a randomized controlled trial (RCT) with a leading technology firm to study how highlighting flexibility and career advancement in job advertisements causally affects the applicant pool. Highlighting career advancement increases the number of applications from men for entry-level positions and attracts additional applicants with strong qualifications and a good fit, which in turn leads to more interview invitations. By contrast, highlighting flexibility increases applications from both women and men at the entry level but provides limited evidence of attracting higher-quality or better-fit applicants. A complementary survey experiment among STEM students shows how job advertisements shape beliefs about the firms job characteristics and work environment. Overall, our results show that the amenities firms choose to highlight can powerfully influence both the size and characteristics of their applicant pool.

title: Difference-in-Kinks Design
affiliations: University of Turku - Turku School of Economics, Labour Institute for Economic Research, Labour Institute for Economic Research and Labour Institute for Economic Research

detail.title: Difference-in-Kinks Design

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Difference-in-Kinks (DiK) design, an econometric framework that extends the standard regression kink design to settings in which the slope of a policy rule varies over time. By combining the key features of the regression kink and difference-in-differences approaches, the DiK design identifies causal effects from variation in kink intensity over time. We formalize both sharp and fuzzy versions of the estimator and derive the identification conditions under a parallel-trends assumption. Applying DiK to Finlands 2011 guarantee pension reform demonstrates that changes in marginal incentives significantly increased the probability of retirement, while the standard regression kink design would have obtained implausibly large estimates in the opposite direction. The DiK design thus offers a flexible framework for policy evaluation in dynamic, nonlinear environments.

title: Does Host Language Proficiency Among Immigrants Reduce Energy Poverty? Evidence from Australia
affiliations: Universidade da Madeira, Universidad Pontificia Comillas and Comillas Pontifical University

detail.title: Does Host Language Proficiency Among Immigrants Reduce Energy Poverty? Evidence from Australia

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Reducing energy poverty is a critical priority for policymakers in both developed and developing nations. Immigrants are often considered a high-risk group due to their heightened vulnerability. While host language proficiency has the potential to mitigate energy poverty among immigrants by enhancing economic integration and facilitating access to essential information and services, its role remains largely unexplored. Using Australian data and addressing endogeneity concerns through a two-stage least-squares (2SLS) approach, this paper presents the first empirical analysis of host language proficiency as a determinant of energy poverty among immigrants. The results show that proficiency in the host language reduces the likelihood of experiencing multidimensional energy poverty by approximately 18.8 percentage points. This effect is partly driven by higher incomes and better access to social assistance among proficient immigrants. The findings underscore the importance of language skills in shaping energy poverty and highlight the need for language education to reduce economic disparities among immigrant populations.

title: The Rise of Robotic Process Automation in Chile: Technological Adoption, Perceptions, and Potential Social Impact in a Post-COVID Economy
affiliations: , Universidad de Playa Ancha and Universitat Internacional de Catalunya

detail.title: The Rise of Robotic Process Automation in Chile: Technological Adoption, Perceptions, and Potential Social Impact in a Post-COVID Economy

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper reviews RPA adoption in Chile and estimates its future social impact. A survey of 103 professionalsmainly from services, mining, and engineeringshows most firms have not begun implementing RPA. Early adopters prioritize strategic alignment, tech readiness, and scalability, citing benefits such as productivity and efficiency, but also challenges like skills gaps, maintenance, and job-loss concerns. Large companies in IT, mining, and services lead post-Covid adoption. Using data from 1.5M firms, the study estimates that full RPA deployment in purchasing could displace up to 75,000 jobs, with a social cost of USD 1B, largely affecting services, commerce, healthcare, the public sector, and engineering. The Metropolitan Region would be most impacted, potentially losing over 45,000 jobs. The findings show how developing economies can adopt advanced technologies while managing social impacts.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how automobile insurers reinterpret statutory duties, procedural requirements, and evidentiary standards during routine liability determinations. Through analysis of statutory frameworks governing safe backing, signaling, comparative fault, and claims-handling obligations in Washington State, the paper argues that everyday administrative practices create a parallel system of "practical law" that diverges from published statutes. Consumers rarely possess the legal knowledge, documentation access, or financial resources to dispute these determinations, while insurers benefit from institutional authority and economic incentives that favor partial fault allocations. The result is a structural dynamic in which insurers can reshape the meaning of law "in the name of the law," quietly reconstructing drivers' duties through routine claims. The paper situates this phenomenon within a broader discussion of regulatory limits, procedural asymmetry, and the gap between written law and applied law in auto insurance systems.

title: Identification and Estimation of Continuous-Time Job Search Models with Preference Shocks
affiliations: Duke University - Department of Economics, , Duke University - Department of Economics and Amazon

detail.title: Identification and Estimation of Continuous-Time Job Search Models with Preference Shocks

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper applies some of the key insights of dynamic discrete choice models to continuous-time job search models. Our framework incorporates preference shocks into search models, resulting in a tight connection between value functions and conditional choice probabilities. In this environment, we establish constructive identification of the model parameters, including the wage offer distributions off- and on-the-job. Our framework makes it possible to estimate nonstationary search models in a simple and tractable way, without having to solve any differential equations. We apply our method using Hungarian administrative data. Longer unemployment durations are associated with lower offer arrival rates, resulting in accepted wages falling over time. Counterfactual simulations indicate that increasing unemployment benefits by 90 days results in a 14-day increase in expected unemployment duration.

title: The Relationship Between Earnings and Sexual Orientation: First Evidence from China
affiliations: Norwegian School of Economics, Department of Economics, , University of Amsterdam - Amsterdam School of Economics (ASE) and Peking University

detail.title: The Relationship Between Earnings and Sexual Orientation: First Evidence from China

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: We document, for the very first time, the relationship between earnings and sexual orientation in China. Using data from the 2020 Chinese Private Life Survey, we find that gay men earn significantly less than comparable heterosexual men, with the largest penalties for rural-hukou holders and among men reporting exclusive same-sex attraction. Lesbian women tend to earn more than heterosexual women, but the differences are small and mostly insignificant. The estimates for bisexual men and women are uniformly insignificant. We conclude that the gay penalties and lesbian premiums in China, albeit imprecisely estimated, mirror those observed in Western labor markets and are most consistent with explanations based on conventional gender norms and intra-household specialization.

title: The Impact of the Far Right on Mainstream Politics: Evidence from the Front National
affiliations: Centre d'Etudes Prospectives et d'Info. Internationales (CEPII),  and Centre d'Etudes Prospectives et d'Info. Internationales (CEPII)

detail.title: The Impact of the Far Right on Mainstream Politics: Evidence from the Front National

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: How does the electoral success of a far-right political force shape the strategies and policy platforms of mainstream candidates? We answer this question by exploiting the political shock of the creation of the Front National, an anti-immigration party, in 1972 and its sudden electoral breakthrough in the 1980s. Through a comprehensive textual analysis of candidate manifestos in French parliamentary elections from 1968 to 1997, we find that right-wing candidates respond to local far-right success, measured as voting shares, by amplifying the salience of immigration in their manifestos. They also adopt more negative positions on immigration and increasingly associate it with issues such as crime and the welfare state. In contrast, the ideological positions of left-wing candidates do not shift in response to far-right electoral gains. We finally show that the strategic adjustments of right- wing candidates help mitigate electoral losses to far-right competitors.

title: Predictive Modeling in Economics: The Role of AI and Deep Learning

detail.title: Predictive Modeling in Economics: The Role of AI and Deep Learning
detail.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence and deep learning techniques in creating models has made great impacts in social economics where intricate phenomenon needs to be modeled and especially forecast. This paper reviews AI techniques and deep learning structures used in the analysis of economic data emphasizing their ability to identify non-linear data characteristics and deal with large number of variables. Some of the areas where this approach is utilized includes; financial forecast, analysis of macroeconomic indicators and assessment of policy outcomes. It also discusses the limitations, including data quality, interpretability, as well as an ethical concern and suggestions for future research works. Consequently, the research underlines the opportunities that AI has within the sphere of economic decision-making, providing accurate and efficient solutions for analysing significant economic issues.

title: Separating Preferences from Endogenous Effort and Cognitive Noise in Observed Decisions
affiliations: École Polytechnique, Paris - Department of Economic Sciences and University of Bonn

detail.title: Separating Preferences from Endogenous Effort and Cognitive Noise in Observed Decisions

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: We develop a micro-founded framework to account for individuals' effort and cognitive noise which confound estimates of preferences based on observed behavior. Using a large-scale experimental dataset we find that observed decision noise responds to the costs and benefits of exerting effort on individual choice tasks as predicted by our model. We estimate that failure to properly account for decision errors due to (rational) inattention on a more complex, but commonly used, task design biases estimates of risk aversion by 50% for the median individual. Effort propensities recovered from preference elicitation tasks generalize to other settings and predict performance on an OECD-sponsored achievement test used to make international comparisons. Furthermore, accounting for endogenous effort allows us to empirically reconcile competing models of discrete choice.

title: Demand for Health Insurance: Financial and Informational Role of Informal Networks
affiliations: University of Warwick, Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Kanpur and University of Calcutta

detail.title: Demand for Health Insurance: Financial and Informational Role of Informal Networks

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study why free public health insurance in India exhibits persistently low utilisation despite high out of pocket health expenses. Using panel data from the Young Lives Survey and the rollout of the Arogyasri scheme in Andhra Pradesh, we distinguish the roles of informal financial and information networks in shaping adoption. Empirically, households embedded in financial networks show higher take-up and utilisation, while information networks have no effect. To explain this pattern, we develop a simple theoretical framework in which informal financial networks act as mutual insurance: because members bear each others uninsured losses, the network has an incentive to push all members to enrol when the expected cost of shocks exceeds enrolment transaction costs. This generates corner solutions for network members and interior solutions for non-members, consistent with observed bimodal take-up patterns. The model clarifies why financialbut not informationalties complement public insurance and highlights community-based mechanisms for increasing adoption.

title: Cost of Capital for Indian Renewable Energy Projects: A Review of Methodologies, Risk Drivers, and Policy Evolution
affiliations: University of Oxford - Smith School of Enterprise and the Environment and University of Oxford

detail.title: Cost of Capital for Indian Renewable Energy Projects: A Review of Methodologies, Risk Drivers, and Policy Evolution
detail.abstract: India's renewable energy sector faces financing challenges that could undermine its 2030 targets, prompting this review of cost of capital dynamics across utility-scale solar and wind projects to address gaps in understanding how financing costs evolve with market maturation and policy intervention. We synthesize evidence from six estimation methodologies, analyse risk drivers through four comprehensive studies, and trace policy evolution across fifteen years, revealing a fundamental tension in cost of capital research where approaches requiring actual project finance data provide high precision, but limited scalability compared to survey methods and financial market proxies that sacrifice accuracy for broader coverage. Historical trends document a complete financing cycle rather than steady improvement, with multiple estimation methods showing WACC compression of 300-400 basis points from 2012-2020 driven by market maturation, followed by 320 basis points expansion through 2024 as global monetary conditions tightened, while wind's historical financing premium over solar has disappeared entirely as both technologies now access identical debt pricing ranges of 8.5-9.75%. Risk analysis across multiple studies consistently points to power purchase agreement counterparty concerns as the most significant financing barrier, reflecting deeper structural problems within India's electricity distribution system where companies face persistent financial distress, accumulating debt of ₹6.84 trillion despite repeated policy interventions, though currency risk has become less material as domestic financial institutions developed greater comfort with renewable energy financing. Policy evolution through four distinct phases successfully tackled many project-level risks, introducing competitive auctions that drove tariff reductions exceeding 80%, yet these technical achievements have been undermined by persistent systemic challenges, with over 50 GW of successfully auctioned capacity now stalled as distribution companies delay signing power purchase agreements, revealing that while India has solved many financing and technical barriers, fundamental distribution sector problems continue to constrain growth, leading us to identify four research priorities: quantifying grid integration financial implications, developing bankability frameworks for storage technologies, evaluating risk mitigation effectiveness, and creating energy policy uncertainty indices.

title: Trading Bloc Financial Integration: With Bloc Currency Units and Trading Bloc Exchange Framework

detail.title: Trading Bloc Financial Integration: With Bloc Currency Units and Trading Bloc Exchange Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this article.

detail.abstract:
This paper outlines a policy framework for establishing a globally integrated financial architecture using a market-based Bloc Currency Unit (BCU) and a Trading Bloc Exchange (TBE). The proposed system enables intra-bloc settlements, cross-currency lending, and financial trading in a stable, non-inflationary digital reserve unit. By drawing upon the experiences of monetary unions and recent innovations in digital currencies, the framework offers a model for achieving monetary sovereignty, financial stability, and macroeconomic coordination within and across trading blocs. The study references findings from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Bank for International Settlements (BIS), and related academic literature on regional currency integration and global liquidity management.

BCUs are issued to member central banks proportional to their gold contribution ratios to the BCB and are freely tradeable currency on the Trading Bloc Exchange (TBE) along with member currencies and dominant external reserve currencies. The BCU functions as the digital reserve currency used exclusively for intra-bloc trade, investment, and financial settlements and is administered by the Bloc Central Bank (BCB), ensuring that bloc reserve currency liquidity remain relatively tied to the BCBs gold reserve assets contributed by member central banks but not constrained by gold market volatility since it is a market-based currency that only uses gold as measure to allocate BCUs to member central banks.

title: Technocratic Dreams, Political Realities: Evaluating Full Reserve Banking for Pakistan

detail.title: Technocratic Dreams, Political Realities: Evaluating Full Reserve Banking for Pakistan
detail.abstract: This paper offers a critical assessment of a recent proposal advocating full reserve banking in Pakistan, inspired by a revival of the Chicago Plan. While rooted in ethical concerns and macroeconomic instability, the paper argues the proposal is best understood as a power-sharing compromise-one requiring a rare balance of power unlikely in Pakistan's current institutional context. Drawing on historical reform efforts and global experiences-including Japan's window guidance and China's state-led finance-the paper outlines why such proposals often fail to materialize. It then proposes a set of pragmatic, culturally resonant reforms grounded in Islamic finance, institutional redesign, and moral legitimacy. Ultimately, it reframes monetary reform not as a technical fix, but as a political struggle over sovereignty, legitimacy, and the public purpose of money-a battle that can be meaningfully fought using tools already at hand.

title: A Long Journey Towards Retirement: A Dynamic Structural Model of Labour Supply and Retirement with Self-Employment

detail.abstract: This article develops a dynamic structural model of older individuals' labour supply decisions that jointly incorporates savings and Social Security claiming. A key innovation is the explicit treatment of self-employment, paid employment, and retirement as distinct career options. Using data from the U.S. Health and Retirement Study, the model shows that self-employment delays retirement and raises labour force participation among married men aged 57-79 by 6.2%p. Estimated elasticities rise sharply with age and vary across sectors, and counterfactual simulations demonstrate that Social Security tax reforms and government-backed self-employment loans enhance retirement security and overall welfare.

title: Monetary Policy and Stock Market Transmission: Evidence from the United Kingdom and India

detail.title: Monetary Policy and Stock Market Transmission: Evidence from the United Kingdom and India
detail.abstract: How does monetary policy transmit differently across advanced and developing financial systems? This paper studies the United Kingdom (1990-2025) and India (2000-2025) using a Structural VAR framework with GDP, CPI, the policy rate, and stock market returns. The results show clear asymmetries. In the UK, monetary tightening raises stock returns in the short run and gradually lowers inflation, while output effects remain modest. In India, the responses of returns, inflation, and output are weak and statistically uncertain, reflecting slower and less effective transmission. Variance decompositions indicate stronger forwardlooking behaviour in UK markets. Monetary policy matters in both economies, but transmission strength depends on financial depth and institutional structure.

title: Author's Approach to Training Staff for Evidence-Based Care

detail.title: Author's Approach to Training Staff for Evidence-Based Care
detail.abstract:
The home care sector for the elderly and people with disabilities is undergoing a momentous structural shift caused by global population aging. This shift is creating both unprecedented commercial demand and an acute systemic crisis in terms of quality and staffing. In the United States (US), people aged 65 and older already account for approximately 17.5% of the total population, and this demographic trend is only intensifying. Given that up to 90% of older Americans express a desire to “age in place” rather than in institutional settings, the demand for high-quality home care services is critical and growing [1].

The growth dynamics of this sector reflect its strategic importance for the national healthcare system. The size of the US home healthcare market in 2025 is estimated at 222.61 billion. It is projected to exceed $644.37 billion by 2034, demonstrating an impressive compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 12.74%. Rapid growth highlights the economic appeal of the industry, but also exposes its fundamental operational shortcomings [2].

Despite its significant commercial potential, the industry faces an acute staffing crisis. The acute shortage of skilled personnel is perhaps the most significant limiting factor for scaling and ensuring quality. In 2025, 59% of home care agencies reported insufficient staffing levels. This problem is exacerbated by extremely high annual staff turnover, which, according to 2024 data, reached 77% at the national level. The main reasons for such high turnover include low wages (the average hourly rate for caregivers is only 15.14) and the lack of social benefits such as health insurance, which less than 20% of employees receive. High staff turnover has a direct impact on the quality of services, as constant changes in personnel make it impossible to create consistent and individualized care plans [1].

In fact, the commercial opportunity in home care (high CAGR) contrasts sharply with operational dysfunction (extreme staff turnover). This indicates that current models of training, staff retention, and quality assurance are structurally inefficient and incapable of sustaining growth. To stabilize the market and improve service quality, radical innovation is needed to ensure rapid and high-quality training of new employees and standardize processes, regardless of the experience of individual caregivers.

title: Capital Allocation Model (CAM): A Multi-Criteria Framework for Oil&Gas Offshore Project Prioritization
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Capital Allocation Model (CAM): A Multi-Criteria Framework for Oil&Gas Offshore Project Prioritization
detail.abstract: The offshore oil and gas industry faces persistent challenges in capital allocation due to high investment requirements, long development horizons, and elevated technical and financial risks. Conventional evaluation approaches, which rely primarily on Net Present Value (NPV) and Internal Rate of Return (IRR), often neglect critical dimensions such as reserve quality, infrastructure interdependence, and portfolio diversification. This narrow perspective has contributed to frequent cost overruns and value erosion in large-scale offshore projects. This paper presents the Capital Allocation Model (CAM), an adaptive MCDM tool that combines financial performance, technical risk, and strategic factors for prioritizing investments. CAM assesses five weighted criteria: NPVsc, EBITDA/CAPEX, CFIR, 1P reserves, and a Technical Risk Score, and applies vector normalization to ensure comparability across heterogeneous KPIs. Strategic orientations (Aggressive Growth, Balanced, Long-Term/Resilience) are operationalized through weight ranges rather than fixed coefficients, aligning rankings with corporate priorities while maintaining auditability. In contrast, the NPV-only approach systematically rewarded projects with high financial returns regardless of risk or reserves, overlooking structural vulnerabilities. CAM provides a more nuanced prioritization: growth-oriented strategies emphasize high-value, high-efficiency projects, whereas resilience-oriented strategies prioritize reserve-rich, lower-risk assets. This adaptability offers executives transparent, scenario-based decision support, enhancing both the defensibility and strategic alignment of capital allocation decisions. CAM's framework is extensible to sectors beyond oil and gas, including renewables, infrastructure, and advanced manufacturing, providing a versatile methodology for investment optimization in uncertain environments. CAM was validated using a simulated portfolio of six offshore projects and benchmarked against a traditional NPV-only ranking. Results demonstrate that CAM not only improves overall portfolio value but also reduces exposure to high-risk assets. Quantitative efficiency metrics confirm its robustness: the Scenario Differentiation Index (SDI) reached 0.72, indicating effective sensitivity to strategic priorities, while the Pareto Efficiency Ratio (PER) was 83%, showing that most top-ranked projects are also non-dominated in efficiency terms. Rank correlations across scenarios (Kendall's τ = 0.68-0.82) further demonstrate a balance between stability and adaptability. To avoid over-interpreting near-ties, we define a practical materiality threshold of ΔScore ≥ 0.02. Rank changes below this gap are labeled "immaterial," ensuring that scenario conclusions reflect meaningful performance differences rather than numerical noise.

title: The Long Shadow of Heroes: Martyrs' Cemetery, Patriotic Education, and Street Crime
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Division of Social Science

detail.title: The Long Shadow of Heroes: Martyrs' Cemetery, Patriotic Education, and Street Crime
detail.abstract: Moving beyond the traditional dichotomy of formal and informal social control, this study explores how state curbs crime by embedding political and historical narratives in physical space. Drawing on geo-coded crime data and a staggered Difference-in-Differences design, results show the establishment of  Martyrs' Cemetery Parks (MCPs) lead to a significant decline of crimes within adjacent areas, especially property crimes. The crime-reduction effect decays with distance and operates through two channels: spatially by the clustering of patriotic education venues rather than more police force, and temporally by seasonally memorial activities especially during the August to October. Moreover, the vignette experiment, complemented by instrumental variable estimates derived from a national survey, provides plausible evidence demonstrating how memorial architecture fosters social order through implicit moral suasion from patriotic education rather than through conventional forms of coercion.

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Corporate Governance Institute – Finance Working Paper No. 1118/2025

detail.abstract: How should firms select and incentivize managers who allocate resources based on private information when their performance is imperfectly measured? We show that, contrary to common wisdom, firms may benefit from appointing managers with misaligned preferences. When performance can be measured more accurately along one dimension than another, firms optimally select managers who are biased toward the poorly measured dimension. This allows to provide strong performance-based incentives on the well-measured dimension while relying on managerial bias to counterbalance substitution effects. As a result, firms with worse performance measurement on some dimension will tend to hire more biased managers, such as managers with strong prosocial or environmental motivations. This framework can explain apparent inconsistencies between firms' stated objectives and the explicit incentives they provide, and it offers a novel perspective on the strategic roles of corporate culture and corporate social responsibility.

title: Leadership and Psychopathy: The Case for Conceptual Discipline

detail.title: Leadership and Psychopathy: The Case for Conceptual Discipline

detail.abstract: The language of psychopathology has become increasingly prevalent in leadership discourse, with terms such as "corporate psychopath" appearing across academic research, practitioner commentary, and popular management literature. This paper argues that psychiatric constructs are frequently extended beyond their legitimate epistemic domains and applied to functional leadership populations without sufficient methodological justification. Drawing on the sociology of diagnosis, medicalization scholarship, and recent work on epistemic fragility in research transmission, the analysis traces how diagnostic drift occurs not only in popular discourse but through secondary academic interpretations and professional summaries that abstract findings from their methodological constraints. The paper proposes the Motivation-Excess-Awareness (MEA) framework as a dimensional alternative to pathologizing models, grounded in established motivational psychology and reflective awareness research. The framework offers concrete guidance for leadership assessment, executive development, and governance design, along with five testable hypotheses for future empirical research. Implications for leadership research methodology, practitioner interventions, and organizational accountability structures are discussed. The analysis calls for greater conceptual discipline and epistemic humility in the use of psychiatric language in leadership studies.

title: Limited Farsightedness in the Housing Matching Model
affiliations: Tilburg University and Tilburg University

detail.title: Limited Farsightedness in the Housing Matching Model
detail.abstract: Myopic solution concepts like the core, the vNM stable set, and the myopic stable set often allow for multiple stable allocations in the housing matching model of Shapley and Scarf (1974). On the other hand, farsighted concepts like the farsighted core, the farsighted vNM stable set, and the DEM farsighted stable set single out the top trading cycle allocation, even irrespective of whether dominations are required to be strict or weak. We address the question of how much farsightedness is needed to obtain the top trading cycle allocation as the unique prediction by studying the horizon-K versions of these solution concepts. The horizon-2 farsighted stable set based on strict dominance is shown to contain the core. In all other non-myopic cases, an allocation is stable if and only if it is the top trading cycle allocation. To facilitate the presentation of our results, we introduce the cycle decomposition of an allocation as a convenient notational device.

No personally identifiable information was collected or analyzed. All data were aggregated at the regional level (cities, counties, and districts). detail.abstract: Despite widespread public attention and funding, homelessness in the United States remains poorly measured and analytically opaque. Over 770,000 people experienced homelessness nationwide in 2024, including 187,000 in California—yet reliable, integrated data remain unavailable for most regions (HUD, 2024). Federal systems capture counts and demographics separately but not together, leaving policymakers without a foundation for evidence-based intervention. HUD's Point-in-Time (PIT) counts enumerate people experiencing homelessness once a year, while U.S. Census surveys describe the broader population but omit tract-level homelessness data and rely on geographies that cannot be directly aligned with PIT regions (HUD, 2024; U.S. Census Bureau, 2024). This disconnect has long prevented data from being used to design, evaluate, or scale interventions effectively. This study produces a geographic and demographic crosswalk between PIT regions and Census tracts across ten California counties, creating a public dataset suitable for machine-learning analysis of regional homelessness. Using this integrated framework, the analysis evaluated how well community demographics explain variation in homelessness rates. Beta regression explained an average of 8% of the variation in regional homelessness rates (mean R² = 0.08, SD = 0.27 across folds) (Ferrari & Cribari-Neto, 2004). Logistic classification distinguished high- versus low-risk regions with 90% ± 7% (SD) ROC-AUC and an F1 of 0.63 ± 0.25 (SD), demonstrating that demographics can identify vulnerability when data are properly aligned. These findings highlight the importance of coherent, interoperable public data for reliable regional analysis.

title: Land Ownership and the Provision of Public Goods: Evidence from Oregon's Forests
affiliations: University of Georgia and University of British Columbia (UBC)

detail.title: Land Ownership and the Provision of Public Goods: Evidence from Oregon's Forests
detail.abstract: Forests generate important public goods, including carbon storage and habitat for biodiversity, while also contributing to increasing wildfire risks. Private landowners do not fully internalize these benefits and risks, potentially leading to socially inefficient management and undersupply of public goods. Exploiting the historical 'checkerboard' land pattern in the American West as an instrument for ownership, we show that public ownership reduces timber harvests and herbicide use in forests, resulting in greater carbon storage, higher biodiversity, and, surprisingly, also lower wildfire risk. These results underscore the role of land ownership in shaping the supply of public goods.

detail.abstract: Early marriage remains a persistent social issue in many developing countries, particularly in South Asia, despite global efforts to discourage the practice. This paper examines early marriage as a harmful custom that violates human rights and restricts long-term social and economic development. Using a mixed qualitative approach, the study draws on secondary literature and semi-structured interviews conducted in rural Sindh, Pakistan. The findings highlight the severe consequences of early marriage, including disrupted education, financial instability, poor maternal and child health outcomes, psychological stress, and increased divorce rates. The study argues that early marriage perpetuates poverty and gender inequality while placing additional strain on national economies. It concludes that stronger legal enforcement, increased access to education, and community-level awareness are essential to reduce the prevalence of early marriage.

detail.abstract: The careful categorisation of conduct is one of the fundamental tasks that courts must perform when interpreting and applying competition law provisions. This contribution makes several points in relation to this idea. To begin with, it defines and explains the pivotal role of categories in the system. It focuses on Articles 101 and 102 TFEU, but the lessons drawn could be easily extended to other areas of EU law Second, it discusses the two main approaches that could be followed to the categorisation of conduct: one that is formal and another one that is substantive (or substance-based). It notes, in this regard, that economic analysis is not only not inimical to this exercise but can greatly contribute to the creation of sound categories. The piece moves, third, to the analysis of the Court’s approach and of the techniques it uses to address and correct frictions and inconsistencies over time.

title: Do Investors Care About Biodiversity Greenwashing?
affiliations: , University of Bamberg and Bamberg University

detail.title: Do Investors Care About Biodiversity Greenwashing?
detail.abstract: We investigate the relation between firms' biodiversity-related disclosures and stock returns and idiosyncratic risk. We use 10-K filings of US listed firms from 2018 to 2024 and text-based measures of biodiversity greenwashing risk. The evaluation is conducted through a customized large language model, with rule-based instructions for assessing the biodiversity disclosures. When considering biodiversity footprints provided by Iceberg Data Lab, we find that companies with high biodiversity impact show lower returns when their disclosure is subject to biodiversity greenwashing risk. We find a similar pattern for the idiosyncratic stock risk. The latter increases when firms with high biodiversity footprint provide disclosure with high biodiversity greenwashing risk. Notably, these results are based on biodiversity footprints adjusted by capital expenditure. The results do not hold when the biodiversity footprint is adjusted by sales. Our interpretation is that investors consider biodiversity risk as a future long-term risk related to long-term investments and not to recent sales. The findings highlight the importance of biodiversity disclosure practices for financial markets, emphasizing the need for standardized reporting frameworks and highlighting potential greenwashing risk faced by investors.

detail.abstract: Background: Public healthcare systems face complex challenges in integrating Generative AI (GenAI) while ensuring trust, accountability, and equity. Aim: This chapter examines how Human-AI Governance (HAIG) frameworks can support the democratic and anticipatory integration of GenAI into the Basque public healthcare system (Osakidetza) through Living Lab experimentation. Method: Using a qualitative action research design, the study combined co-design workshops, focus groups, and ethnographic observation with general practitioners (GPs) and patients in a primary care context, supported by BioGipuzkoa. Results: Findings identified five interdependent factors shaping trustworthy GenAI adoption: epistemic uncertainty and clinical judgment, trust and explainability, accountability and error, data ownership and consent, and digital divides and access. Contribution: The chapter demonstrates how Living Labs can serve as a practical HAIG instrument-operationalising anticipatory governance, enabling participatory oversight, and offering a replicable methodology for other regions seeking to integrate GenAI responsibly into public healthcare. Conclusions: The study concludes that embedding GenAI within HAIG-informed Living Lab infrastructures in Osakidetza and BioGipuzkoa can strengthen augmentation of clinical judgment, multi-layered explainability, shared accountability, participatory data governance, and inclusion-thereby providing a concrete pathway for the democratic and anticipatory integration of GenAI in public healthcare systems that is elaborated in Section 6.

detail.title: Labor Supply and Savings Responses to Increasing the Pension Eligibility Age in South Korea
detail.abstract: We study how South Koreans responded to an increase in the full pension eligibility age. Using a regression discontinuity design, we document the causal effects of the change on several potential margins of adjustment. We find clear evidence of delayed benefit claiming, consistent with studies in other settings. However, we find little to no statistical evidence of changes in labor supply, in contrast with previous literature. We also find no changes in savings or spending. These muted responses may be, in part, because the South Korean pension is relatively new and benefit replacement rates are comparatively modest.

detail.title: The ESG-Carbon Performance Disconnect: Implications for Sustainable Investing
detail.abstract: Using ESG ratings and full-scope emissions data for S&P 500 firms, we document a sharp ESG-carbon performance disconnect among sector peers. Despite strong correlations across E/S/G pillars, ESG scores are unrelated to firms' current or future carbon intensity and instead reflect disclosure and management processes. To assess the investment implications, we construct sector-neutral variants of the S&P 500 index that tilt toward sector peers with high ESG scores or low carbon intensity. While both strategies deliver similar returns, ESG-tilting increases portfolio emissions by 12%, whereas carbon-tilting reduces emissions by 40%. ESG-based investing thus distorts capital allocation without advancing decarbonization.

title: Reducing Food Prices and Improving Nutrition in India: Short-Term Dietary Shifts and Long-Term Food Wastage Solutions

detail.title: Reducing Food Prices and Improving Nutrition in India: Short-Term Dietary Shifts and Long-Term Food Wastage Solutions
detail.abstract: Rising food prices and persistent malnutrition remain major challenges in India despite improvements in agricultural production and public distribution systems. Evidence from the National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) Household Consumption Expenditure and Nutritional Intake Surveys indicates that a large share of Indian households-across income groups-face dietary imbalances characterized by excessive dependence on cereals, inadequate protein intake, low dietary diversity, and significant food wastage. These challenges contribute to undernutrition among low-income households and lifestyle-related health issues among middle-and high-income groups, while also exerting upward pressure on food prices. This working paper proposes a two-pronged policy framework to address these issues. First, it presents short-term dietary shifts through affordable, nutritionally balanced food patterns tailored to low-, middle-, and high-income households. Using NSSO data as a benchmark, the proposed food patterns demonstrate that improved nutrition-higher protein intake, better fat quality, and greater micronutrient diversity-can be achieved at equal or lower monthly food expenditure, particularly for low-and middle-income groups, while simultaneously reducing household-level food wastage. Second, the paper outlines long-term food wastage reduction strategies, focusing on systemic inefficiencies in storage, transportation, mandi operations, and post-harvest management. The proposed framework emphasizes digital monitoring of food flows, strengthened government mandis, improved coldchain infrastructure, and farmer training to minimize post-harvest losses and stabilize food supply. Overall, the paper argues that coordinated dietary reform at the household level, combined with institutional reforms in food distribution and wastage management, can reduce food prices, improve nutritional outcomes, and enhance food system efficiency in India. The findings aim to contribute to policy discussions on food security, nutrition, and sustainable consumption.

title: The Climate Impact of U.S. LNG Exports in Coal-to-Gas Substitution: Evidence from a Bayesian Meta-Analysis of Methane Leakage Rates

detail.title: The Climate Impact of U.S. LNG Exports in Coal-to-Gas Substitution: Evidence from a Bayesian Meta-Analysis of Methane Leakage Rates
detail.abstract: The U.S. is the world's largest producer and exporter of liquefied natural gas (LNG). Exported LNG may displace coal in other countries, which may in turn lead to a net reduction in greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Methane emissions in the LNG supply chain are a key determinant of the net GHG impact of exported LNG over its lifecycle. I collect 58 point estimates from 28 studies spanning more than a decade of data collection and 7 estimating methods, and perform a multi-level Bayesian meta-analysis to estimate methane emissions rates in 11 oil and gas producing basins, accounting for nearly 90% of U.S. gas production. I apply the meta-analysis results to compare the GHG emissions of exported LNG sourced from each basin, to coal in Asia assuming perfect substitution. I find that under conservative scenarios, substituting Asian coal for U.S. LNG produced from at least 3 of the 11 basins studied (accounting for 28% of total production) would increase net GHG emissions.

title: Regulating Money Market Fund in the USA and in the EU: Open Issues and New Perspectives

detail.title: Regulating Money Market Fund in the USA and in the EU: Open Issues and New Perspectives
detail.abstract: This paper examines the regulatory architecture governing money market funds (MMFs) in the United States and the European Union, adopting a comparative and functional perspective that situates MMFs as “special” mutual funds combining investment-fund features with money-like characteristics. After reconstructing the historical evolution of US regulation—from the adoption of Rule 2a-7 to the 2023 amendments prompted by the COVID-19 market turmoil—the analysis contrasts it with the EU framework established by Regulation (EU) 2017/1131, highlighting both convergences and persistent divergences in regulatory design. Particular attention is devoted to unresolved issues within the European MMF regime, including the role of credit ratings and internal credit assessments, the prudential function of “know-your-customer” policies, stress-testing obligations, and the categorical prohibition of external support. The paper argues that these differences reflect not only distinct historical trajectories but also deeper systemic and institutional choices concerning financial stability and the boundary between banking and asset management. Finally, building on the functional parallels between MMFs and certain crypto-assets, the paper explores the extent to which the prudential logic embedded in the MMFR could inform future developments in the regulation of electronic money tokens and asset-referenced tokens under MiCAR, especially in addressing liquidity risk and run-like dynamics at scale.

declarations.funderStatement: This project has received funding from the European Unions’s Horizon 2020 research and innovation programme under the grant agreement No. 695945.

detail.abstract: We use a randomized controlled trial (RCT) to examine the causal effect of information provision on household electricity consumption. Households were randomly assigned to one of two conditions. The information condition (N = 457) received feedback on their electricity consumption via a smartphone app, while the control group (N = 454) did not have access to the app. Electricity consumption was tracked for up to 70 weeks post-treatment and up to 3 weeks pre-treatment. Using data from Google Analytics, we can distinguish between the intent-to-treat group (all app recipients) and those who actively engaged with the app (and thus effectively received the information treatment). Our analysis yields three main results. First, we identify a statistically significant intent-to-treat (ITT) effect, with households in the treatment group reducing their electricity consumption by an average of 5%. Second, the ITT effect underestimates the true savings for households that actively engage with the app. We find that households with higher engagement levels achieve substantially greater reductions in electricity consumption than those with lower engagement. Third, we observe long-term reductions in electricity consumption even as app engagement declines over time. Statistically significant savings persist for up to 30 weeks after treatment. Beyond this period, the effect stabilizes at a lower level of consumption, but is no longer statistically significant.

detail.title: Assessing the Learning and Teaching Preferences among Undergraduate Economics Students
detail.abstract: This study delved into the experiences of undergraduate economics students at the University of Rwanda with online learning during the COVID-19 pandemic. Qualitative data was collected from 283 students through a structured questionnaire administered in August-September 2021. Findings revealed a spectrum of student attitudes, with a notable proportion expressing dissatisfaction. Factors such as technological infrastructure, pedagogical methods, and socioeconomic disparities influenced student satisfaction and perceptions of online learning's efficacy. Students demonstrated a preference for kinesthetic learning and emphasized the importance of student agency. However, challenges related to technology access, financial constraints, and inadequate online support significantly impacted student experiences. These findings underscore the need for diverse pedagogical approaches, addressing the digital divide, and continuous evaluation of online learning practices to improve student outcomes. Further research is essential to comprehensively understand the complex interplay of factors influencing student experiences in this evolving educational landscape.

The findings demonstrated that implementing new technologies will improve business performance for Malaysia's logistics sector and that organizational, technological, and environmental factors have a major impact on the implementation of technological breakthroughs.

title: Big in Japan: The Design and Limits of Japan's Mobile Software Competition Act

detail.title: Big in Japan: The Design and Limits of Japan's Mobile Software Competition Act
detail.abstract: Japan’s Mobile Software Competition Act, also known as the Smartphone Act, entered into force on 18 December 2025. It establishes an ex ante regulatory framework in relation to mobile operating systems, app stores, browsers, and search engines. Apple and Google have been designated as companies subject to the new rules. The Act is rooted in a diagnosis of oligopoly across different layers of the smartphone ecosystem and in the perceived limitations of ex post Antimonopoly Act enforcement. It also reflects Japan’s desire to align with emerging global regulatory trends. Its substantive rules—largely similar to those in the DMA—are paired with a distinctive enforcement architecture combining extensive guidelines, reporting duties, dialogue-based supervision, and possible sanctions. Safety concerns played a central role in shaping the Act: Japan rejected mandatory side-loading and embedded broad security- and privacy-related justifications. The Act has been received more calmly internationally than the DMA, yet Japan’s highly consensual, non-adversarial enforcement culture raises questions about whether the new framework will deliver meaningful behavioural change from Google and Apple.

title: Does Machine Learning really Help to Select Mutual Funds with Positive Alpha?

detail.title: Does Machine Learning really Help to Select Mutual Funds with Positive Alpha?
detail.abstract: We revisit the recent finding of DeMiguel, Gil-Bazo, Nogales and Santos (2023) that machine learning (ML) methods can identify long-only portfolios of actively managed mutual funds with positive net annual alpha of up to 2.69%. Using their replication package, we show that these conclusions are driven by a coding error that introduces a forward-looking bias in the construction of portfolio returns. Removing the bias eliminates the longonly alpha. Based on an independent replication, we find that nonlinear ML methods consistently identify underperforming funds. However, this also holds for linear models. Consequently, long-short portfolios deliver robust and economically meaningful alphas, driven predominantly by the short leg. We further extend the analysis by expanding the sample period to the end of 2024, by considering forecast horizons up to 36 months and conducting univariate sorts across fund characteristics. These extensions do not materially enhance long-only predictability but offer empirical evidence of the relative advantages of ML at longer horizons. Overall, our results suggest that ML adds value primarily through the consistent avoidance of poorly performing funds rather than by identifying long-only outperforming ones. This has important implications for both the academic interpretation of ML performance and its practical application in active mutual fund selection.

detail.title: Machine Learning and Micro-Prudential Climate Stress Testing
detail.abstract: Rising climate-related transition risks demand more robust risk management tools. This paper introduces a novel climate stress testing framework that applies machine learning methods to examine firm-level carbon price shocks. The framework extends existing approaches by explicitly modelling small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and incorporating prediction uncertainty via conformal prediction. We estimate that a EUR 100 carbon price shock nearly doubles the number of loss-making firms and triggers an increase in loan defaults by 7.9%. These effects are significantly amplified by shock size. SMEs are disproportionately affected, whereas large corporations show greater resilience. Substantial uncertainty remains due to limited emissions reporting, particularly among SMEs. Overall, the results underscore both the value of machine learning for enhancing the granularity and reliability of climate stress tests and the need for more comprehensive firm-level climate disclosure.

title: Choosing the Stage: The Strategic Role of Disclosure Venues in Guidance Revisions

detail.title: Choosing the Stage: The Strategic Role of Disclosure Venues in Guidance Revisions
detail.abstract: This study examines whether managers strategically choose how to communicate guidance revisions, exploiting institutional variation across three disclosure venues-guidance calls, investor conferences, and analyst/investor (A/I) days. Firms with higher litigation risk and larger negative news tend to gravitate toward calls, while those facing analyst disagreement and delivering modest news tend to prefer conferences and analyst/investor (A/I) days. Using textual analysis, we document that managers systematically frame identical guidance news differently across venues: calls feature cautious, litigation-conscious language, regardless of the news content, while conferences and A/I days employ optimistic framing, even when delivering negative updates. Consistent with strategic communication, venues are also associated with different market outcomes: calls amplify investor reactions to negative news and effectively reset expectations downward, as evidenced by more favorable subsequent earnings surprises following negative guidance. Conferences and A/I days achieve consensus-building through muted market reactions and reduced analyst dispersion; however, the optimistic framing leads to more negative subsequent earnings surprises. Our findings reveal that venue choice constitutes a distinct strategic dimension in corporate communication.

title: The Forgotten Friction: How the "Smallest Coin Problem" Amplified the Great Depression

detail.title: The Forgotten Friction: How the "Smallest Coin Problem" Amplified the Great Depression
detail.abstract: This paper challenges the conventional wisdom that the severity of the Great Depression was driven solely by psychological or macroeconomic policy failures. We argue that a long-overlooked techno-physical factor—the hard, physical indivisibility of the "smallest coin" in the era's monetary system—acted as a crucial "deflationary amplifier." Through a detailed analysis of newly unearthed primary newspaper archives from the 1930s, we provide robust historical evidence for this thesis. We demonstrate that the "smallest coin problem" was not a theoretical curiosity but a real, severe, and intractable crisis, forcing states to issue "sales tax tokens" to plug significant fiscal holes and creating immense market friction at the micro-level. These frictions, as documented in contemporary reports of chaotic commerce and public complaint, systematically exacerbated the downturn by raising transaction costs, distorting price signals, and increasing economic uncertainty. The ultimate result was a "monetary deadlock"—a paradoxical state of coin shortages in the streets coexisting with stagnant, unwanted inventory in the U.S. Mint's vaults—which we identify as the final, tragic outcome of this amplification process. This historical re-reading carries profound implications. It suggests that the dreaded "Keynesian deflationary spiral," in its most catastrophic form, is a historical artifact of an obsolete monetary technology. Consequently, the infinite divisibility native to modern digital currency is not merely an incremental convenience but a paradigm-shifting revolution that permanently decommissions this amplifier. Our findings call for a fundamental re-evaluation of the modern, near-universal policy mandate to "fight deflation at all costs," a mandate predicated on a fear that may no longer have a technological basis.
